title: Dual-Task and Limited Capacity Laboratory
summary: Do two simple tasks alone, then both at once. Measure the cost against your own single-task baseline, and see whether it falls evenly on the two.
learningObjectives: Measure a dual-task cost against its own single-task baseline.
Read an asymmetric cost and say what question it raises.
Predict what happens when the second task no longer needs a choice response.
Distinguish a general-capacity account from a structural bottleneck by their predictions.
Explain why multitasking ability cannot be inferred from one short run.
interactionTypes: enforced block order with a stage track
counting version with a single end-of-block report
results withheld until each block ends
bar chart paired with a data table
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; response times and answers stay in the browser tab as JavaScript variables and disappear on reload, and nothing is written to storage.
accessibilityNotes: No display is ever timed out - each waits for its response - and nothing on the page animates or transitions, so there is nothing for a reduced-motion setting to switch off. Only the two glyphs change; the panel, its size and its position stay put. The number sits directly above the letter and both are centred, so neither task needs an eye movement to reach the other. Responses are by pointer or by the keys printed on the buttons (F and J for the letter, D and K for the number, space for the counting version), each button carries an explicit accessible name, and the key hint itself is aria-hidden decoration. Response targets are 3.25rem tall. Nothing depends on colour: the stage track marks the current block with a border, a background and aria-current=step as well as a number; chart bars print their own values and the combined bars are hatched as well as differently filled; all results are numbers in a table. The trial display is aria-hidden during a block because a live description would state the answer. The chart is aria-hidden and paired inside the same figure with a six-column table. Every control has an accessible name, headings do not skip, focus moves to the results heading, and forced-colours rules are supplied for the display, the answered-state marker and both chart series. Usable at 320px and at projector widths with no horizontal page scroll; the wide results table scrolls inside its own container.
readmeTopic: Dual-task costs: baselines, asymmetry, and why multitasking is not a trait
simulationNotes: The learner's own blocks are real responses, not simulated. A block is 20 trials; the inter-trial interval is 500 ms and no display is timed out. Letters are drawn 50/50 from vowels and consonants; numbers are a single digit 1-9 in the easy setting and a two-digit number 12-98 judged on the parity of its digit sum in the hard setting, which adds processing without changing the response set. In the counting version there is no per-item choice response: block 2 is paced by a single non-choice Next press, which gives a viewing time per number, and in block 3 the number is on screen for exactly as long as the letter response takes, so no separate number time is reported there and the informative number measure is the count itself. Correct responses between 200 ms and 4000 ms enter the means; errors, anticipations and lapses are counted and reported separately. Block 3 always follows blocks 1 and 2, so the cost is measured against baselines collected when the learner was less practised - a confound the design cannot remove, stated in those words in the limits panel. The worked example is one simulated participant who ran both settings, with RT = base + Normal(0, 80) + Exponential(mean 55) floored at 220 ms. Set A (respond mode, easy, seed 20260971, 60 trials per block) uses bases 610/780 for letters and 570/850 for numbers with accuracies .97/.93 and .96/.90, and produces a cost of +130 ms to letters and +273 ms to numbers. Set B (counting mode, easy, seed 20260972) uses bases 610/690 for letters and 700 for the number viewing time, with counting errors of 0 alone and 2 in the dual block, and produces a letter cost of +98 ms. The asymmetry in Set A and the much smaller letter cost in Set B are built in to illustrate the shape of the classic findings; they are not evidence for them, not norms and not anybody's data. Browser display and input timing are uncontrolled.
